title: Two Tables, One Truth
subtitle: Connect the pizza orders to customer names
conceptSummary: INNER JOIN connects two tables on a matching column (key). Only rows with matches in BOTH tables appear.

dialogue.text: Welcome to the Join District! Here, two tables become one. The orders table has customer_id but not the customer's name. The customers table has the name. We need BOTH!
INNER JOIN. Match customer_id in orders to customer_id in customers. Only rows with a matching ID in BOTH tables appear.

teachMoment.title: INNER JOIN: Connecting Tables
teachMoment.body:
An INNER JOIN merges two tables on a shared column:

SELECT o.order_id, c.name, o.total_price
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id

• o and c are aliases for the table names (shorthand!)
• ON specifies which columns to match
• Only rows where customer_id exists in BOTH tables appear

task.instruction: Join orders and customers to show the customer name, order date, and total price for all orders.
task.startingQuery:
SELECT c.name, o.order_date, o.total_price
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
task.solution: SELECT c.name, o.order_date, o.total_price FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id

hints.text: Both tables share customer_id. Use that as the ON condition.
Pattern: FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
SELECT c.name, o.order_date, o.total_price FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id

winDialogue.text: Now we can see Priya Sharma's orders directly. No more decoding customer IDs!
And I see some customers in our database who have ZERO orders. We need a LEFT JOIN for that.

storyBeat: With joins, we can now see the full picture. A customer exists in the database with no orders — but their credentials were used to place SHADOW42 orders. Ghost account detected!
